score_reasons.agency: Never blocked; but with six points always full I was rarely asked to choose.
score_reasons.realism: The reveal comparison to the real shoal is good; months 3 to 5 were unrelated crises and a seat projection for a one-party state.
score_reasons.replay: Replay same opening is clear, but I saw no reason to try other choices since Accept all won.
score_reasons.recommend: I would show it to a friend for the title screen and the reveal, with a warning about the middle.

score_reasons.fun: Four months in I was approving the staff's picks; the result cards are fun to see, the decisions are not yet tense.
score_reasons.clarity: Plenty of explanation, but five counters for one resource and disagreeing numbers undermine it.
score_reasons.visual: Title, result illustrations and typography are crafted; cramped cards, an overflow and a text-heavy desk drag it down.
score_reasons.feels_like_a_game: The title and result scenes feel authored; the desk feels like an admin panel with Choose buttons.
score_reasons.agency: I always knew what to press, but 'Choose all recommended' then Execute makes my input nearly optional, and Skip means different things.
score_reasons.realism: Plausible Scarborough dynamics, but a one-party leader quoted about ballot boxes felt templated.
score_reasons.replay: I would not start a second run until the numbers agree; I did not play a second game.
score_reasons.recommend: I would tell a friend the art is better than they expect, with a warning that the UI is busy. Not yet 'crafted game', no longer 'AI dashboard'.

rounds.quit_point: Month 3 (Jan 2027) desk: after pressing Choose all recommended and Execute without reading a card, I realised the loop was clicking through, and the capital counters disagreed again. I played one more month to finish the record.
rounds.verbatim: Better than I expected from a title screen, and then the desk turned into a form. Pick one number for my political capital and make every screen agree with it.
